correctness.rationale: On fixed k≥0 and 0<a<b, the ratio sequence r in [a,b]^N uniquely reconstructs p by the displayed factorial normalization. The summable majorant k! b^n/[n!(n+k)!] proves TV continuity and all exponential moments (and locally uniform convergence for the complex moment-generating series); inverse coordinate continuity uses positivity of every p_n. Under the transform the factorial terms cancel, a common factor r₀ disappears, and the ratios shift exactly. Finite repeated words give dense periodic orbits with all least periods; finite alphabet subsystems give unbounded entropy. The concatenation of all binary words by length visits each finite cylinder arbitrarily late; for independent full-support letters a countable cylinder basis and independent block trials give the claimed almost-sure visits. Constant sequences are exactly the fixed points in the ratio domain. Shift convergence to a constant or to prescribed periodic phases is equivalent to the corresponding scalar tail or residue limits; finitely many residue classes exhaust all subsequences. For the stated TV bound, the weight quotients lie between (1−ε)^n and (1+ε)^n; convexity gives 1−(1−ε)^n≤(1+ε)^n−1. Normalization costs at most the unnormalized ℓ¹ difference divided by the first mass, which is at least D_s(1−ε); analyticity gives O(ε). The illustrated explicit 2,1/2 example belongs to intervals containing both symbols; every nondegenerate [a,b] has its own alternating example. The checker and verification notes were inspected, not executed, and finite checks are not used for the infinite-time or all-law conclusions.

value.rationale: The result answers a natural iteration question raised by an exact Stein fixed-point characterization: positive Bessel fixed points need not attract even within a stable compact class with all exponential moments. It describes precisely when they do, gives explicit periodic and nonconvergent mechanisms, and quantifies approximation by a periodic orbit in the metric used for convergence. These consequences on an invariant family are stronger than just producing one nonfixed law or restating the known transform.
